title: The Life of a Star
objective: After this level you can read a star's temperature from its color and outline how the Sun will end.
summary: Stars are born in clouds of gas and dust. Blue stars are hottest, red coolest. The Sun will become a red giant and then a white dwarf; massive stars can go supernova.

cards.headline: Stars have a life story: birth, a long middle age, and a very dramatic ending.
Color is temperature
cards.body: Look closely and stars have colors. Blue-white stars are the hottest; red stars are the coolest. The Sun sits in between, which is why it looks white-yellow.

events.label: Forms from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust
Fusing hydrogen into helium in its core
Sheds its outer layers and ends as a white dwarf

cards.headline: Bigger stars, bigger endings
cards.body: The Sun won't explode. But stars much more massive than the Sun can end their lives in a supernova — an explosion that can briefly outshine a whole galaxy.

cards.headline: Stellar life cycle: unlocked
learned: Blue stars are hotter than red stars
Stars form in clouds of gas and dust
The Sun will become a red giant, then a white dwarf
Massive stars can end as supernovae

questions.prompt: How will the Sun most likely end its life?

options.label: As a red giant, then a white dwarf
Exploding as a supernova, then a black hole
options.rationale: The Sun isn’t massive enough to explode.

options.label: Collapsing straight into a black hole
options.rationale: The Sun isn’t massive enough for that.

options.label: It will keep shining unchanged forever
options.rationale: It will run short of hydrogen in its core.

questions.explanation: In about 5 billion years the Sun will swell into a red giant, then shrink into a white dwarf.

questions.prompt: A star looks blue-white. What does that tell you?
questions.explanation: A star's color reveals its surface temperature: bluer means hotter.

questions.prompt: From Level 2: when the Sun swells into a red giant, what is it running low on?

options.label: Hydrogen to fuse in its core
Oxygen to keep its fires burning
options.rationale: The Sun doesn’t burn; it fuses hydrogen.

options.label: Helium to fuse in its outer layers
options.rationale: Helium builds up as hydrogen fuses; it’s hydrogen that runs short.

options.label: Heat from the surrounding galaxy
options.rationale: A star makes its own energy.

questions.explanation: A star shines by fusing hydrogen in its core. When the Sun's core runs short of hydrogen, it changes, swelling into a red giant.
